Brasier’s success wasn't solely limited to the 3x3 Rubik's Cube. He also excelled in solving other variations, including the 4x4 and 5x5 cubes. He consistently ranked highly in these events, showcasing his versatility and deep understanding of cube mechanics and solving techniques. He held the world record for the 4x4 cube for a period in 2007 with a time of 22.86 seconds.

However, the landscape of speedcubing began to evolve. The rise of new generations of cubers, employing more advanced techniques and utilizing increasingly sophisticated cube designs, began to challenge Brasier's dominance. While he continued to compete and achieve respectable results, he didn' "quite recapture the peak performance he displayed in the mid-2000s. Brasier’s career wasn’t solely defined by competition. He became a respected figure within the speedcubing community, known for his analytical approach to solving and his willingness to share his knowledge with other cubers. He contributed to the development of new algorithms and techniques, further demonstrating his deep understanding of the sport. He also became involved in the design and manufacturing of speedcubes, collaborating with companies to refine cube mechanics and improve performance.

After a period of reduced competitive activity, Brasier made a notable return to the spotlight in 2018. He participated in the World Cube Championship, demonstrating that despite a period of absence, his skills hadn’t diminished.  He officially retired from competitive cubing in 2023, citing a desire to focus on other aspects of his life. Currently, he works as a software engineer at Google in Seattle, leveraging his analytical skills in a different field. While his competitive speedcubing career has concluded, Ryan Brasier’s legacy as a pioneer and influential figure in the world of speedcubing remains secure, a testament to his dedication, skill, and impact on the sport.

title: Marcel Hernández
text:
Marcel Hernández González was born on June 19, 1983, in the small town of Santa Bárbara de Goiás, Goiás, Brazil. His parents, José and Maria Lúcia Hernández, were modest farmers, and Marcel grew up on their family farm, experiencing a rural upbringing centered around agriculture and a close-knit community. He wasn't initially destined for a career in football; his early passions involved music and playing the guitar, a hobby he continues to enjoy. However, the prevalence of football in Brazilian culture, and the encouragement of local coaches, eventually led him to pursue the sport.

His football journey began at the age of 11 when he joined the youth ranks of Atlético Goianiense, a prominent club in the state of Goiás. He quickly demonstrated a natural talent, possessing a powerful shot and a keen eye for goal. He progressed through the youth system, eventually making his debut for the senior team in 2002, at the age of 19. His initial appearances were sporadic, mostly as a substitute, but he gradually established himself as a reliable option in the squad. In 2003, he scored his first professional goal for Atlético Goianiense, contributing to the team’s efforts in the Campeonato Brasileiro Série C.

A significant turning point in his career arrived in 2005 when he transferred to São Paulo Futebol Clube, one of Brazil’s biggest and most successful clubs. This move provided him with a larger platform and increased exposure. At São Paulo, he faced intense competition for playing time, but he persevered and proved his worth, contributing to the team’s campaigns in the Copa Libertadores and Campeonato Brasileiro Série A. He scored crucial goals during this period, including vital strikes in continental competitions.

Hernández’s consistent performances attracted attention from abroad. In 2008, he made a move to Europe, signing with Eredivisie side Vitesse Arnhem in the Netherlands. This marked the beginning of a successful and relatively long spell in European football. He quickly became a fan favorite at Vitesse, scoring frequently and demonstrating his ability to adapt to a different style of play. Over six seasons with Vitesse, from 2008 to 2014, he scored a remarkable 72 goals in 138 league appearances, establishing himself as one of the league's top strikers. His prolific goalscoring earned him numerous accolades, including the Eredivisie Golden Shoe in the 2011-2012 season.

Following his successful tenure at Vitesse, Hernández transferred to FC Twente in 2014. While his time at Twente was shorter, he continued to score goals, contributing to the team's efforts in the Eredivisie. In 2016, he joined Beitar Jerusalem in Israel, where he had another productive period, scoring 23 goals in 33 league games during the 2016-2017 season.

After a short stint in Cyprus with APOEL FC in 2018, Hernández returned to Brazil in 2019, joining Avaí FC. He then had a brief spell with Londrina Esporte Clube before returning to Atlético Goianiense in 2021, completing a full circle in his professional career. He announced his retirement from professional football on December 6, 2023, at the age of 40, citing recurring knee injuries as the primary reason.

Throughout his career, Marcel Hernández amassed impressive statistics. He scored over 200 professional goals across various leagues and competitions. Beyond the numbers, he was known for his work ethic, determination, and his ability to deliver crucial goals in high-pressure situations. He holds the record for the most goals scored by a foreign player for Vitesse Arnhem. He is remembered by fans in the Netherlands and Israel as a prolific striker and a dedicated professional.

Since retiring, Hernández has expressed interest in coaching and working within the football community in Goiás. He remains connected to his hometown and family, regularly returning to Santa Bárbara de Goiás. He continues to play recreational football and enjoys spending time with his wife, Ana Paula, and their two children. His legacy is one of perseverance, adaptability, and a remarkable goalscoring record that cemented his place as a respected figure in Brazilian and European football.

title: Maggie Cogan
text:
Margaret “Maggie” Cogan (née O’Connell) was a pioneering figure in British radio broadcasting, particularly renowned for her work in children’s programming and her innovative use of sound effects. Born on 12th June 1907 in Cork, Ireland, she was the eldest of six children to Patrick O’Connell, a railway clerk, and his wife, Mary (née O’Flynn). Her early life was steeped in Irish storytelling traditions, a formative influence that would later inform her approach to radio drama. The family emigrated to England in 1918, settling in Battersea, London, where her father found work as a railway signalman.

Cogan's formal education was limited, attending Battersea Grammar School for a short period before leaving at the age of 14 to support her family by working as a typist. She initially worked for a shipping company, then moved to a solicitor's office. Her interest in theatre began during this time, attending plays whenever possible and participating in amateur dramatic productions. In 1927, she married William Cogan, a carpenter, and they had two daughters, Maureen (born 1930) and Patricia (born 1932).

Cogan's broadcasting career began unexpectedly in 1937. She responded to an advertisement in *The Times* for a “sound effects artist” at the BBC. Initially, her role was to create everyday sounds – footsteps, doors closing, the clinking of glasses – using a wide range of objects and props. She quickly proved to have a remarkable talent for recreating complex soundscapes, demonstrating a meticulous attention to detail and an innate understanding of how sound could evoke atmosphere and emotion. Her early work involved mimicking sounds for news bulletins, drama productions, and even orchestral pieces, often using household items like pots, pans, and lengths of pipe. It’s estimated she had a repertoire of over 300 distinct sounds.

The outbreak of World War II significantly expanded Cogan’s role. The BBC's foreign language services required realistic sound effects to accompany broadcasts aimed at occupied Europe, and Cogan's skills were invaluable. She became instrumental in creating the sound of German tanks, aircraft, and military drills, crucial for maintaining morale and providing information to resistance movements. She worked tirelessly throughout the war years, often under pressure and with limited resources.

Following the war, Cogan’s career shifted decisively towards children’s programming. In 1947, she joined the BBC’s Children's Department, where she quickly established herself as a leading figure. She created and produced numerous radio dramas and serials aimed at young listeners. Her most famous creation was “The Secret of Bluebell Wood,” which began in 1952 and ran for over 100 episodes over a decade, captivating generations of children with its blend of adventure, fantasy, and gentle humour. The series, featuring a group of children who discover a magical wood, was characterized by its intricate sound design, with Cogan crafting a rich tapestry of woodland sounds, magical effects, and distinctive character voices. She didn't just create sounds; she often contributed character voices herself, alongside a cast of established actors.

Beyond "Bluebell Wood," Cogan produced and directed other popular children’s series such as “The Twins” and “Wendy’s Adventures.” She was a strong advocate for high-quality children’s programming, believing that radio could be a powerful tool for education and entertainment. She championed the use of imaginative soundscapes to engage young listeners and to bring stories to life.  Her methods were innovative; she frequently used multiple layers of sound, carefully balancing dialogue, music, and sound effects to create a fully immersive experience.

In the 1960s, Cogan moved into television, contributing to children’s programmes like "Watch Out!" and "Jackson’s Corner," bringing her expertise in sound design to the visual medium.  She retired from the BBC in 1972 after 35 years of service.

Margaret Cogan died on 27th November 1995, at the age of 88, in Surbiton, Surrey.  While she didn’t seek public recognition, her influence on British radio and children’s programming is undeniable. Her legacy lies in the countless hours of enjoyment she brought to generations of listeners and in her pioneering work in the art of sound design, which continues to inspire sound artists today. Though largely uncredited in contemporary broadcasts, her meticulous craft and imaginative approach helped shape the sound of British radio for decades.

title: Ricky Martin
text:
Ricardo Martin Lizotte, known professionally as Ricky Martin, was born on December 24, 1971, in San Juan, Puerto Rico. His father, Enrique Martin, was a tennis coach and his mother, Dolores Lizotte, was a housewife. He grew up in Dorado, Puerto Rico, a municipality near San Juan. Martin's childhood was marked by a strong artistic inclination; he began taking singing and dancing lessons at the age of six, initially with the encouragement of his grandmother, Grace Lizotte. This early training proved foundational to his future career.

At age twelve, Martin was selected to join the Puerto Rican boy band Menudo. He replaced Ricky Melendez in 1984 and adopted the stage name Ricky Martin. Menudo was a hugely popular group throughout Latin America and the United States, known for their catchy pop tunes and youthful appeal. Martin remained with Menudo for five years, participating in numerous tours, recording several albums, and experiencing considerable commercial success. He contributed to albums like "Explosion" (1985), "Dominando el Mundo" (1986), and "Emociones" (1987), and participated in the film "Menudo: La Historia" (1986). By the time he left Menudo in 1989, he had already sold over 12 million albums worldwide with the group.

Following his departure from Menudo, Martin pursued a solo career, initially focusing on acting. He appeared in several Puerto Rican and Mexican telenovelas, including "Daniela" (1992) and "Secreto de Amor" (1995). However, his musical ambitions remained strong, and he began recording his first solo album, "Ricky Martin" in 1991. While this album had some success in Latin American markets, it didn't achieve widespread recognition.

The turning point in Martin's career came in 1997 with the release of “Vuelve” (Return). The album, produced by Kike Santander, featured hits like "María" and "La Descarga," which topped the Latin charts and earned him a Grammy Award nomination for Best Latin Pop Album. This album sold over 6 million copies globally, establishing him as a major force in Latin music.

His breakthrough into the mainstream English-speaking market occurred in 1999 with the release of "Livin' la Vida Loca," the lead single from his English-language album, "Ricky Martin." The song, a collaboration with the Black Eyed Peas’ will.i.am, became an international phenomenon, reaching number one on the Billboard Hot 100 chart and propelling the album to multi-platinum status. “Ricky Martin” sold over 15 million copies worldwide.  He followed this success with the album "She Bangs" (2000), which also achieved significant commercial success and further cemented his status as a global superstar. He performed at the Super Bowl halftime show in 2000 alongside NSYNC and Britney Spears, reaching an estimated audience of over 100 million viewers.

Throughout the 2000s and 2010s, Martin continued to release albums in both English and Spanish, including "Sound Loaded" (2003), "Almas del Silencio" (2003), and "Música de Hoy" (2011). He has received numerous accolades, including four Grammy Awards, five Latin Grammy Awards, and several MTV Video Music Awards.  He has sold over 80 million records worldwide, making him one of the best-selling Latin artists of all time.

In 2018, Martin publicly came out as gay, a significant moment for him and the LGBTQ+ community. He has since become an advocate for LGBTQ+ rights and equality. He married Syrian-American artist Jwan Yosef in 2017, and they have four children together: twin sons Valentino and Matteo, born in 2008 via surrogate, and two daughters, Lucía and Renn, born in 2019 and 2021 respectively.

Beyond his music career, Martin has also been involved in philanthropic endeavors, supporting various charitable organizations focused on children's welfare and LGBTQ+ rights. He continues to tour and record music, demonstrating a sustained commitment to his artistry and a desire to connect with audiences worldwide. In 2023, he received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, a recognition of his enduring contribution to the entertainment industry.

title: Kathinka Pasveer
text:
Kathinka Pasveer was born on 29 August 1949, in Medan, North Sumatra, Indonesia. Her parents, Pieter Willem Pasveer and Johanna Elisabeth de Bruin, were both Dutch civil servants working for the colonial administration. Pieter Willem Pasveer (1916-1987) held a position in the Department of Public Works, and Johanna Elisabeth de Bruin (1922-2011) worked in the Department of Education. Kathinka was the eldest of three children; her younger siblings are Willem Pieter Pasveer and Elisabeth Johanna Pasveer. Her early childhood was spent in Medan, a city then experiencing significant social and political upheaval as Indonesia moved toward independence. The family returned to the Netherlands in 1954, settling in The Hague.

Kathinka Pasveer attended the Gemeentelijk Lyceum in The Hague, completing her gymnasium education in 1967. She subsequently enrolled at Leiden University, studying Dutch language and literature. She obtained her Bachelor of Arts degree in 1972, followed by a Master of Arts degree in 1975, both from Leiden University. Her Master's thesis, "De Constructie van de Romantische Held in de Nederlandse Romantiek," focused on the portrayal of the romantic hero in Dutch literature.  This demonstrated an early interest in literary theory and analysis that would inform her later career.

Pasveer began her professional career at the Dutch Institute for War Documentation (NIOD) in Amsterdam in 1976. Initially employed as a research assistant, she quickly progressed to become a research fellow, focusing primarily on the experiences of Dutch civilians during the Second World War.  Her work at the NIOD was pivotal in shifting the historical narrative surrounding the war, moving beyond a solely military perspective to incorporate the perspectives of those who lived under occupation. She became a leading expert on the Dutch resistance movement and the impact of the war on everyday life.

A significant achievement during her time at the NIOD was her work on the "Verzuimoproep" (Call-up Notice) project, commencing in 1984. This ambitious project involved the systematic analysis of over 150,000 individual files documenting Dutch citizens who were mobilized for forced labor in Germany during the Second World War.  This painstaking research, involving a team of researchers and volunteers, led to the publication of “Tussen hoop en vrees: Nederlanders in Duitse werkkampen 1942-1945” (Between Hope and Fear: The Dutch in German Work Camps 1942-1945) in 1991, a groundbreaking study that provided a detailed and nuanced understanding of the lives and experiences of these individuals. The book was widely praised for its meticulous research and its sensitive portrayal of the human cost of the war.

In 1995, Kathinka Pasveer transitioned to the Huygens Institute for Dutch History (Huygens Instituut), where she remained until her retirement in 2014. At the Huygens Institute, she continued her research on the Second World War, expanding her focus to include the post-war period and the process of national remembrance. She played a key role in the development of digital resources for Dutch historical research, contributing to the online publication of archival materials and the creation of interactive historical maps. She also mentored numerous junior researchers, fostering a new generation of historians.

Pasveer’s contributions to Dutch history were recognized with several awards and honors. In 2004, she received the Gerard Aalders Prize, a prestigious award given annually for outstanding contributions to Dutch historical research.  She was also a member of the Royal Netherlands Historical Society and served on various advisory boards for museums and historical institutions.  Her publications, including numerous articles and chapters in edited volumes, are widely cited in the field of Dutch history.

Kathinka Pasveer retired from the Huygens Institute in 2014, but remained actively engaged in historical scholarship. She continued to lecture and participate in public discussions about the Second World War and its legacy. She lives in Amsterdam and remains a respected figure within the Dutch historical community. She has consistently advocated for a more inclusive and nuanced understanding of Dutch history, emphasizing the importance of individual experiences and perspectives. Her meticulous research and insightful analysis have left a lasting impact on the field, ensuring that the stories of ordinary people during extraordinary times are not forgotten.

title: Cha Eun-woo
text:
Cha Eun-woo, born Lee Dong-hyuk (이동혁) on May 10, 1997, in Gunpo, Gyeonggi Province, South Korea, is a multifaceted entertainer recognized for his singing, dancing, acting, and visual appeal. His stage name, Cha Eun-woo, is a combination of his family name, Cha, and a shortened form of his birth name, Dong-woo. He hails from a relatively ordinary background; his father, Lee Ho-seong, is a retired military officer, and his mother, Choi Mi-kyung, is a homemaker. He has an older sister, Lee Ji-hye, who is married and has a son, Cha Woo-jin, whom Eun-woo affectionately refers to as his nephew and often features in his social media.

Eun-woo’s interest in performing arts began during his middle school years, initially with drawing and then shifting to dance. He was scouted by Fantagio Entertainment, a Korean entertainment agency, while waiting for a bus at a bus stop in Seoul in 2011. After undergoing a year of training, he officially joined the agency in 2012. During his training period, he focused on vocals, dance, and acting, demonstrating a quick aptitude for all three disciplines.

His debut occurred on June 6, 2014, as a member of the five-member boy group ASTRO. The group's name, ASTRO, is an acronym for "Add Stellar to Your Road," reflecting Fantagio’s vision for the group to guide and inspire their fans. ASTRO released their debut single, "Hide Me," and quickly gained recognition for their synchronized performances and catchy music. Eun-woo played a significant role within the group, contributing to vocals and dance routines and showcasing a natural stage presence. ASTRO continued to release numerous singles and EPs, including "Breathless" (2015), "Summer Vibes" (2016), "All In" (2016), "Baby Baby" (2017), "Promise" (2018), "Blue Flame" (2019), and "All Yours" (2021).  Their discography spans genres from pop and R&B to dance and ballad.

While maintaining his commitments to ASTRO, Cha Eun-woo simultaneously pursued acting opportunities, demonstrating impressive versatility. His initial acting role was a minor appearance in the drama "Aftermath" in 2014. A significant breakthrough came in 2015 with his role as Choi Eun-pyo in the historical drama "The Best Hit." However, it was his role as Lee Dong-jae in the popular webtoon-based drama "My ID is Gangnam Beauty" (2018) that propelled him to widespread recognition and solidified his status as a rising actor. The drama garnered significant viewership both domestically and internationally, and Eun-woo’s portrayal of the gentle and charming Dong-jae earned him considerable praise. He subsequently starred in "Island" (2019) and "True Beauty" (2020-2021), further expanding his acting repertoire and demonstrating his ability to portray diverse characters. "True Beauty," in particular, achieved immense popularity, showcasing his romantic chemistry with co-star Moon Ga-young.

Beyond acting and music, Cha Eun-woo has also engaged in hosting duties. He co-hosted the music show “Weekly Idol” from 2018 to 2020, demonstrating his wit and engaging personality. He also frequently participates in variety shows and interviews, endearing himself to audiences with his polite demeanor and thoughtful responses.

Eun-woo's popularity has resulted in numerous endorsements and brand ambassadorships, including partnerships with luxury brands like Sulwhasoo and Dior. He has also been recognized for his visual appeal, frequently topping lists of the “most handsome men” in South Korea and internationally. In 2020, he was named a global ambassador for Davidoff, a Swiss fragrance and tobacco company.  He has amassed a significant following on social media platforms, with millions of followers on Instagram.

As of 2023, Cha Eun-woo is currently fulfilling his mandatory military service, having enlisted on May 22, 2023, at the Nonsan Recruit Training Depot.  He is expected to serve as a social worker, utilizing his gentle nature and public image for community support. While on leave for ASTRO’s 9th anniversary on June 6, 2024, he expressed his determination to return to performing after completing his service. His future plans include continued acting projects and musical endeavors, solidifying his position as a beloved figure in the Korean entertainment industry.

title: Carl Braun (obstetrician)
text:
Carl Victor Braun was a highly influential German obstetrician and gynecologist, renowned for his contributions to the understanding and treatment of ectopic pregnancies and his pioneering work in the development of amniocentesis. He was born on March 2, 1882, in Greiz, Thuringia, Germany, to Carl Braun, a district judge, and his wife, Luise (née Köhler). His early education took place in Greiz and subsequently in Weimar, where he attended the Classical Gymnasium. Demonstrating a strong aptitude for science, he pursued his medical studies at the Universities of Tübingen, Berlin, and Kiel, completing his doctorate in 1906 at Kiel with a dissertation on the innervation of the uterine cervix.

Following his doctorate, Braun served as an assistant at the Institute for Physiological Research in Kiel under Professor Wilhelm Erbstein, a leading figure in neurology. This period honed his research skills and instilled in him a rigorous scientific approach. In 1909, he transitioned to the women's clinic at the Charité Hospital in Berlin, under the direction of Professor Theodor Leisering, a prominent figure in obstetrics. This appointment marked the beginning of his dedicated career in obstetrics and gynecology. Braun rapidly distinguished himself through his clinical acumen and research interests, becoming an assistant physician in 1911.

Braun's most significant and enduring contribution to medicine centered around ectopic pregnancies. Prior to his work, the diagnosis of ectopic pregnancies – pregnancies occurring outside the uterus, most commonly in the fallopian tube – was notoriously difficult and often delayed, leading to high maternal mortality rates due to rupture and internal bleeding. Braun, through meticulous clinical observation and a large series of cases, recognized the characteristic symptoms and developed a diagnostic approach that significantly improved the chances of early detection and successful surgical intervention. His landmark publication, “Über extrauterine Schwangerschaften” (On Ectopic Pregnancies), published in 1912, synthesized his findings and presented a clear diagnostic algorithm. This work, which described 158 cases of ectopic pregnancy, became a standard reference for obstetricians worldwide and fundamentally changed the management of this life-threatening condition. It significantly reduced mortality rates and paved the way for improved surgical techniques.

Beyond his work on ectopic pregnancies, Braun was a pioneer in the field of amniocentesis. In 1922, he published a paper detailing a technique for amniocentesis – the procedure of puncturing the amniotic sac to collect amniotic fluid – for diagnostic purposes. While earlier attempts at amniocentesis existed, Braun’s procedure was notably safer and more reliable, utilizing a finer needle and meticulous technique to minimize the risk of complications. Initially, he used amniocentesis primarily to assess fetal lung maturity, particularly in cases of premature labor, but its potential for prenatal diagnosis was quickly recognized. The development of amniotic fluid analysis for chromosomal abnormalities and other genetic conditions built directly upon Braun's foundational work.

Braun’s reputation grew steadily, and in 1925 he was appointed as the director of the women’s clinic in Düsseldorf. He held this position until his retirement in 1952. During his tenure in Düsseldorf, he continued to refine his surgical techniques and expanded the clinic's research activities. He was a dedicated teacher and mentor, training numerous generations of obstetricians and gynecologists. He received numerous awards and honors throughout his career, recognizing his significant contributions to the field. These included honorary degrees from several universities and membership in prestigious medical societies.

Carl Braun married Margarete Müller in 1913; they had one son, Karl-Heinz.  He remained active in medical affairs and research even after his retirement. He died on February 13, 1969, in Düsseldorf, at the age of 86. His legacy endures as a pivotal figure in the history of obstetrics, whose dedication to clinical observation and rigorous scientific inquiry transformed the understanding and treatment of ectopic pregnancies and laid the groundwork for the development of prenatal diagnostic techniques that continue to benefit women and children today. His meticulous approach and detailed documentation of clinical cases set a standard for medical research that continues to inspire.

title: Lodewicus du Plessis

Lodewicus Christiaan du Plessis, commonly known as Lod, was a prominent South African rugby player and administrator, best remembered for his significant contributions to the Springboks and the development of rugby in South Africa during the mid-20th century. He was born on May 12, 1917, in Paarl, Cape Province, South Africa, to Pieter Willem du Plessis and his wife, Johanna Dorothea de Bruyn. He was one of eight children in the family. His early life was steeped in the culture of the Boland region, known for its strong rugby traditions. He attended Paarl Boys' High School, a renowned rugby-producing school, where he first demonstrated his athletic talent.

Du Plessis’s rugby career began in earnest at Western Province, a key rugby province in the Cape. He initially played as a flank and occasionally as a lock. His performances quickly drew attention, and he was selected for the Western Province team in 1938. The following year, in 1939, marked a pivotal moment as he was chosen to represent the Springboks in their tour to Argentina. This tour, while short due to the outbreak of World War II, provided him with his first taste of international rugby. He played in all three test matches against Argentina, showcasing his strength, skill, and determination.

The war interrupted his playing career, and he served with the South African forces, specifically the 6th Artillery Regiment, from 1940 to 1945. He saw action in North Africa and Italy, experiencing the hardships of war firsthand. Despite the disruption, he maintained his fitness and remained connected to rugby whenever possible. Upon his return to South Africa in 1945, he immediately resumed his involvement with Western Province rugby. He played for Western Province until 1951, accumulating a significant number of caps and consistently performing at a high level.

His national career resumed in 1947 when he was selected for the Springboks’ tour to Britain, Ireland, France and Belgium. This tour was particularly significant as it included a series of test matches against the top European rugby nations. Du Plessis played in all five test matches, cementing his reputation as one of the best locks in the world. He was known for his tenacious tackling, his ability to dominate scrums, and his leadership on the field. The Springboks won the series against England (3-0), Ireland (2-0) and drew with Wales (1-1), marking a successful tour.

Following his playing career, du Plessis transitioned into rugby administration. He served as a selector for Western Province from 1953 to 1960. He was then appointed as a selector for the Springboks from 1960 to 1968, a period during which the Springboks achieved considerable success, including a series victory against the British & Irish Lions in 1962, and a drawn series against New Zealand in 1965. His role as a selector was crucial in shaping the composition of the Springbok teams during this era, often navigating the complexities of player selection within the context of the apartheid regime. He was known for his integrity and commitment to fair selection practices, although the system itself was inherently flawed due to the racial policies of the time.

In 1968, du Plessis reached the pinnacle of his administrative career when he was elected chairman of the South African Rugby Board (SARB), the governing body of rugby in South Africa. He served in this position from 1968 to 1973. During his tenure, he faced increasing international pressure to end the policy of racial segregation in South African rugby. While he did not actively challenge the apartheid policies, he attempted to manage the escalating crisis and maintain South Africa's participation in international competition. He was a staunch defender of the status quo, and his chairmanship coincided with growing isolation of South African rugby from the rest of the world.

Lod du Plessis retired from his position as chairman of the SARB in 1973. He remained involved in local rugby administration for several years after that. He married Elsie Maria van der Merwe on April 22, 1948, and they had three children: two sons, Pieter and Christiaan, and a daughter, Sonja. He died on December 12, 2008, at the age of 91, in Paarl, where he spent most of his life. He is remembered as a dedicated rugby player and administrator who left a lasting legacy on the sport in South Africa, albeit one inextricably linked to the controversial political landscape of his time.

title: Shawn Ashmore
text:
Shawn Robert Ashmore was born on October 17, 1974, in Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada. He is the elder of two children born to Kent Ashmore, a former Royal Canadian Air Force mechanic and later a businessman, and Donna Ashmore, a homemaker. His younger brother, Aaron Ashmore, also became a successful actor, and the two have maintained a close relationship throughout their lives and careers. Shawn’s early childhood was spent in Millbrook, Nova Scotia, before the family moved to Brampton, Ontario, when he was seven years old. It was in Brampton that Shawn and Aaron began their acting careers, initially as child models and appearing in various commercials.

The Ashmore brothers’ early acting work was largely in Canadian television. Shawn’s first credited television role was in 1988 in an episode of the CBC series *Street Legal*. He continued to accumulate smaller roles throughout the late 1980s and early 1990s, appearing in shows like *Degrassi High* (1991), *L.A. Law* (1993), and *Forever Knight* (1995). Aaron, following closely behind, similarly began appearing in television productions around the same time. This period of consistent, though often minor, roles honed their skills and provided valuable experience in the industry.

A significant turning point in Shawn’s career arrived in 1996 with his casting as Craig Manning in the Canadian teen drama *Degrassi: The Next Generation*. He played the role for five seasons, from 2000 to 2005, becoming a central figure in the show's early years and gaining widespread recognition. Craig Manning’s storyline, which dealt with mental health struggles, including bipolar disorder, was particularly impactful, and Ashmore received praise for his portrayal. *Degrassi: The Next Generation* proved to be a launchpad for numerous young actors, and Ashmore’s profile rose considerably as a result.

While still involved with *Degrassi*, Ashmore began to secure roles in American productions. In 2002, he appeared in the film *Convenience* and the television movie *My Brother’s Keeper*.  However, his most prominent role outside of *Degrassi* came in 2006 when he was cast as Tim Slater in the Fox science fiction series *The Flash*.  This role, playing a speedster with a troubled past, significantly expanded his audience and showcased his action capabilities. He appeared in 22 episodes across the show's two seasons, which ran from 2006 to 2007.

Following *The Flash*, Ashmore continued to work steadily in television and film. He had recurring roles in series like *Smallville* (2007-2011), playing extrasensory perception expert JC Denton, and *Warehouse 13* (2010-2011), as Peter Stone.  He also appeared in the Syfy original movie *Proof of Lies* (2011) and the horror film *Stay* (2013).  In 2014, he joined the cast of *Covert Affairs* for its final two seasons, portraying Jake Lassiter.

Beyond acting, Ashmore has demonstrated a commitment to charitable causes. He has been involved with organizations supporting mental health awareness, reflecting his experiences with the portrayal of bipolar disorder in *Degrassi*. He has also supported various animal welfare organizations.

Shawn Ashmore married Annie Woodley, a makeup artist, on August 17, 2013, in Ontario, Canada. They have two children, a daughter born in 2016 and a son born in 2019. As of 2023, Ashmore continues to act, appearing in television movies and smaller film projects. While he hasn’t had a major television series role since *Covert Affairs*, he remains active in the industry and continues to leverage his experience and versatility. His career, spanning over three decades, demonstrates a consistent dedication to his craft and a resilience in navigating the evolving landscape of the entertainment industry, all while maintaining a strong family life and connection with his brother, Aaron.

title: Sila María Calderón
text:
Sila María Calderón Fouchet was born on July 14, 1948, in San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Rafael Calderón López and Josefina Fouchet Toro. Her father, Rafael Calderón, would later serve as Governor of Puerto Rico from 1969 to 1973. Her upbringing was steeped in politics and public service, affording her early exposure to the challenges and responsibilities of leadership. She attended the Colegio Sagrado Corazón in San Juan, graduating in 1966. She then pursued a degree in Business Administration at the University of Puerto Rico, Río Piedras campus, completing her studies in 1970.

Calderón's professional career began in the private sector. Following her graduation, she worked as an accountant for the firm of Rivera & Co. for a short period. However, her commitment to public service quickly drew her toward government roles. In 1973, she joined the Department of Economic Development and Planning under Governor Rafael Hernández Colón, serving in various capacities, including as Executive Director of the Puerto Rico Industrial Development Company (PRIDCO) from 1977 to 1980. During her time at PRIDCO, she was instrumental in attracting foreign investment and fostering economic growth within the island, overseeing the creation of numerous industrial parks and incentivizing businesses to establish operations in Puerto Rico.

A pivotal moment in her career came in 1981 when she was appointed Secretary of Economic Development and Planning by Governor Fernando Luis Ribas Dominicci. She held this position until 1984, continuing her efforts to stimulate the Puerto Rican economy and promote job creation. In 1984, she became the first woman elected to the Puerto Rico Senate, representing the District of San Juan. She served in the Senate until 1992, focusing on issues related to economic development, education, and women's rights. Her legislative work included advocating for increased funding for public schools and supporting legislation aimed at promoting gender equality.

In 2000, Calderón made history as the first woman elected Governor of Puerto Rico. Running as the candidate for the Popular Democratic Party, she secured 51.3% of the vote, defeating Pedro Rosselló, the incumbent New Progressive Party candidate. Her governorship, which lasted from 2001 to 2005, was marked by a focus on social programs, education reform, and economic development. She prioritized initiatives aimed at reducing poverty and improving access to healthcare.  One key initiative was the "Plan Pueblo a Pueblo," a program designed to provide social services and economic opportunities to underserved communities.  She also implemented reforms in the education system, aiming to improve student performance and teacher training.  During her tenure, Puerto Rico experienced periods of economic challenges, including budget deficits and rising unemployment, requiring her administration to implement austerity measures.  While criticized by some for these measures, she maintained that they were necessary to ensure the island’s fiscal stability.

After leaving office in 2005, Calderón remained active in public life.  She served on the board of directors of several organizations, including the Puerto Rico Chamber of Commerce. In 2012, she was appointed by President Barack Obama to the United States President's Commission on Educational Excellence for Hispanics. She served on this commission until 2015, contributing to the development of recommendations aimed at improving educational outcomes for Hispanic students nationwide.

In more recent years, Calderón has focused on philanthropic endeavors and supporting community initiatives. She has been a vocal advocate for Puerto Rican statehood, aligning herself with the New Progressive Party on this issue in recent years, a shift from her traditional Popular Democratic Party affiliation.  She has also been actively involved in relief efforts following natural disasters that have impacted Puerto Rico, including the devastating Hurricane Maria in 2017. As of 2023, she resides in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and continues to be a recognized figure in the island’s political and social landscape, leaving behind a legacy as a pioneering woman in Puerto Rican politics and a dedicated public servant. She is married to Dr. José Antonio Ferrer Rubias, and they have two children, Rafael and José.
